reading.rtitle: Two launches, one month -- and only one of them is still on the shelf
paras: In March, two products were sitting in the same room, on the same table, waiting for the same decision. Both had the same budget. Both had a campaign ready. The first one was a sauce for families, and the second was a premium line for restaurants. The company launched both of them within four weeks of each other, and today only one of them is still on the shelf. The interesting part is that nobody in that room could have told you which one it would be.

The sauce moved first, and it moved because of somebody else. While the team was preparing the launch for the fifteenth of May, a competitor announced almost exactly the same product on the ninth of March. The room decided in two days to move the date forward by six weeks. It was the right decision and the wrong preparation. They were testing two packaging designs in two cities at the time, and that test was never finished. They picked design B because it was the one on the table on the day they had to choose.

Then came the part that hurt. The campaign ran nationally, in nine states, from the first of April. The stock was ready in two. People were walking into stores and asking for the product by name, and the shelf was empty, so they bought something else and did not come back. Awareness doubled in eight weeks, which is an excellent number, and sales in the first month were forty percent under the plan, which is a terrible one. Both numbers are true and they describe the same campaign.

The premium line did the opposite, and it did it quietly. It rolled out in two states only, with half the advertising, and the stock was in every store on day one. It grew slowly for five months, and then a retail chain gave it shelf space in a third state because customers were already asking for it. Nobody wrote a case study about it. The lesson of both launches fits in one line, and the retail buyer said it better than the marketing team did: it is better to be small and full than national and empty.
reading.source: Internal launch review -- marketing and sales

listenings.text: All right, I will tell you what actually happened, and I am not going to make it sound better than it was. In March we were testing two packaging designs, in two cities, and the test had about three weeks to go. That is what we were doing when the competitor announced almost exactly our product, on the ninth. Two days later we decided to move the launch forward by six weeks. I still think that was the right decision, and I also think it was the wrong preparation, and both of those things can be true at once. We picked design B because it was the one on the table on the day we had to choose, not because the data told us to. Now, the numbers. Awareness doubled in eight weeks. Doubled. That is the best awareness result this brand has ever had and I am proud of it. And sales in the first month came in forty percent under the plan. Those two numbers are describing the same campaign, and I have spent two months understanding why.

Let me tell you how this looks from where I stand, because it is very simple and nobody in marketing seems to enjoy hearing it. I give a new product shelf space and I give it twelve weeks. If it does not sell in twelve weeks, the space goes to somebody who will sell. That is not personal, that is arithmetic. Now, what happened with your launch. Your advertising was excellent. People were coming into my stores and asking for the product by name in week one, which almost never happens, and the shelf was empty, because the stock was in two states and the campaign was in nine. So they bought the competitor, and here is the part that costs you: they did not come back the following week to check again. You spent the money on the hardest thing, which is making somebody want it, and then you were not there. My advice, and I have given it to four companies this year: roll it out slowly. Two states first. It is better to be small and full than national and empty.
